title: Barecare
subtitle: Full-stack work across a six-service cosmetics commerce platform: shop, warehouse, B2B and influencer systems.
description: Barecare sells 2,100+ Korean and Japanese cosmetics products in Bulgaria. As part of the engineering team I build features across the storefront and admin, the warehouse system, a B2B shop and an influencer platform, and the SDKs that connect them.
overview:
Barecare is a cosmetics retailer running its online shop, physical shop, warehouse, B2B sales and influencer programme on a set of Laravel services that talk to each other through shared SDKs.

I work across all of them. My 240+ commits since December 2025 span six repositories, from the checkout and in-store order flow to warehouse stock states and the APIs that let the services create orders and users in one another.
problem: Each part of the business runs on its own service, so most features cross a boundary: an order placed in the shop has to exist in the warehouse, a B2B order has to check real stock, an approved influencer needs an account in the main platform. Keeping those systems consistent is most of the work.
approach: I build features end to end (database changes, service logic, the API or SDK call to the neighbouring service, and the admin or storefront interface) and add the checks that catch it when two systems disagree.
contributions: In-store order flow rebuilt in Alpine.js with barcode scanning, cash and card payments, and MyPOS card-terminal integration
Order ↔ warehouse synchronisation, status history and discrepancy flags when the two systems disagree
B2B order creation from CSV/XLSX uploads, with a preview and a warehouse availability check before anything is created
Shop inventory receiving with barcodes and expiry dates, stock adjustments and order returns
Product search and catalogue improvements, search translations, structured SEO metadata and a reorderable category tree
Warehouse system: item statuses moved to a state machine, coming-stock deliveries and receiving, priority and customs statuses, short-expiry warnings
Query optimisation on the warehouse purchase-order listing to remove duplicate queries
Cross-service APIs: creating orders and internal users between the shop, warehouse and influencer platform through shared SDKs
B2B shop: expiry and broken-stock flags, warehouse expiry sync, customer-group inventory rules and SKU-level Excel exports

title: Walk Out
subtitle: A productivity platform that turns focus, reading and habits into progression, with real stakes if you want them.
description: My own startup, in active development: a React app on a Laravel API that tracks deep work, reading, study and screen time, turns it into XP, streaks and leagues, and lets people back their goals with money or friends.
overview:
Most productivity tools record what you did and move on. Walk Out keeps it: every focus session, chapter read and goal hit feeds a profile that levels up, keeps streaks and competes in leagues.

Under the hood it is a versioned REST API with around 85 models and 112 migrations behind a React front end.
approach: The backend is organised by domain (productivity, reading, study, movement, screen time, social, staking, verification), each with its own controllers, services and tests, all behind one versioned API with a consistent response envelope.
solution: A Laravel 12 API secured with Sanctum, with queued jobs and scheduled tasks for evaluations, and a React 19 front end built with Vite, Tailwind CSS and Motion.

title: Winna Coffee
subtitle: A redesign that turned a template-style export site into an editorial farm profile for roasters.
description: A redesign of the export website for Winna Trading PLC, which grows and exports shade-grown Arabica from its own farm in Southwest Ethiopia. The original site, built by another developer, looked like a generic template; the new one presents the farm the way specialty-coffee buyers evaluate it.
overview:
Winna exports green coffee from the Nibo Sendeka farm in the Sheka Zone. Their buyers are roasters abroad, so the website has to work like a farm profile: where the coffee is grown, how, and what makes it different, with a clear path to request samples or a quote.

They already had a site, built by another developer. I redesigned it from the ground up.
solution: A single-page React and TypeScript site with full-bleed farm photography, a detailed farm profile (area, mapped blocks, coordinates, altitude, rainfall, soil), the varieties grown, the process from cultivation to export, and persistent quote and WhatsApp actions.
features: Farm profile with area, block structure, location, coordinates and growing conditions
Varieties section presenting each Arabica selection grown on the farm
Step-by-step process from cultivation to direct export
Persistent “Request a quote” and WhatsApp contact actions
Responsive layout for buyers browsing on phones

approach: Start from what a roaster wants to know before asking for a sample, and let the farm itself carry the design: real photography from Nibo Sendeka, editorial serif typography, and the farm data presented as a proper profile rather than a list of claims.

title: Affordly
subtitle: A mortgage readiness analyser for people whose income changes every month.
description: A local-first tool I built for myself: import your real income history as a CSV and it tells you whether a mortgage is safe, borderline or risky, and why, using stress tests, a transparent readiness score and nothing ever uploaded.
overview: A normal mortgage calculator answers “what will my payment be?”. Freelance income doesn't fit that question. Affordly answers “given my actual, irregular income, when would this mortgage be reasonable, and why?”, and shows every number behind the answer.
problem: Averages hide the months that hurt. A freelancer can earn well on average and still miss payments in lean months, so affordability has to be judged against the real shape of the income, not one number.
approach: Keep the financial engine as pure, tested TypeScript, completely separate from React, and make every output explainable: each score component shows its weight and the figure behind it.
solution: A React 19 and TypeScript app with a calculation layer covering income analysis, an exact amortisation schedule, affordability ratios, stress testing and a readiness score, all running in the browser, saved only to local storage.

title: Backtest Viewer
subtitle: An analysis dashboard for Freqtrade trading-bot backtests, built to catch results that are too good to be true.
description: A personal tool for my algorithmic-trading research: drop in Freqtrade backtest files and compare strategies across equity, drawdown, fees, exit reasons and monthly returns, with warnings when a backtest can't be trusted.
overview: Freqtrade's built-in reports are text tables. I wanted to see strategies side by side, over any date range, and to know when a result was inflated by how the backtest was run, so I built two viewers that read backtest files directly in the browser.
features: Load backtest .zip or .json files, or scan a whole results folder at once
Compare multiple strategies with a date-range slider and year presets
Equity curves, real drawdown and time underwater
Exit-reason, fee-impact, per-pair and monthly heatmap breakdowns
Warnings for backtests run without intrabar detail, which can inflate results
A second “Realism” viewer that models money across exchanges over time

decisions.title: Deploy only the viewers
decisions.description: The viewers live inside the bot's working folder, so the deployment ignores everything except the HTML files, so API credentials, strategies and market data never reach the host.
